articles.title: Twelve gift ideas for hosts so you never show up to the party empty-handed
articles.summary: Put down the grocery store carnations and give your host a token of appreciation they will love. The best holiday gifts – obsessively tested by the Guardian US. The golden rule of holiday party going is simple: never show up empty-handed.
body: Thankfully, you don’t have to spend a fortune when choosing a hostess gift – especially since many of us tend to have multiple parties to attend. “I think bringing a small gift for your host or hostess is such a thoughtful gesture, especially during the holidays when so much time and care goes into welcoming family and friends,” said Shauna Varvel, author of Provence Style and owner of Le Mas des Poiriers, a farmhouse estate in Provence. “It’s a simple way to show your appreciation, and it doesn’t have to be extravagant to feel special.”

Nick Leighton, co-host of the etiquette podcast Were You Raised By Wolves?, suggests bringing something that will not give your already-busy host more work. “Flowers that need a vase? Something that has to go into the oven or freezer? Something you expect them to serve or pour at their party? All not great choices,” he said.
So before you head out for holiday party season, take a gander at these thoughtful, original gifts that will let your host or hostess know you really care.

articles.title: ‘Opposites don’t attract’: Adam Grant on how to strengthen friendships and make new ones faster
articles.summary: The organisational psychologist and bestselling author says learning about the four types of platonic bonds can help us understand our relationships. Here’s a stat to ruin your day: of all the people you would call a friend, research suggests only about half would reciprocate.
body: The thought might make you want to wipe your contacts list and start afresh. But let’s look on the positive side, suggests Adam Grant, the Wharton organisational psychologist and New York Times bestselling author of Originals, and Hidden Potential.

“It means there’s some people that we don’t think of as friends, who see us as friends – so we may have more potential connections out there than we realise,” Grant says. The trick, he adds, is to understand the part these relationships play in our lives, the wavelength we share and what they need to thrive.

In his new book Vibe: The Secrets of Strong Connections in a Lonely World, Grant describes four platonic bonds: associates (transactional ties, who exchange resources), allies (who align on purpose and compatible goals), pals (who have the same idea of fun, and how to have a good time) and companions (connections based on care).

People can belong to more than one category, but understanding why we connect can help us to strengthen existing bonds and forge new ones faster, Grant says. It also helps us to let go of unrealistic expectations.

articles.title: Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button | Adrian Chiles
articles.summary: Not even a compelling TV drama can stop me from staring at my phone. But this urge started 40 years ago, with what was at first presented as a useful feature. I blame the shuffle button.
body: I blame the shuffle button. That’s what started me on the long road to a thoroughly scattered mind – generally unable to focus on anything for more than a few minutes or even seconds. I was always a bit like this, hence an ADHD diagnosis in later life. But back in the day I still managed to read a lot of books, watch long films and listen to whole records at one sitting. Now? Not so much. Actually, hardly ever.

Even something on television that I’m really engaged in – a drama or a football match – can hold me for only a few minutes before I find myself scrolling on my phone looking for I know not what. I don’t know whether it’s because I’m drawn to the small phone screen, or rather that I find absorption with whatever I’m watching on the big flatscreen just too much to bear.

articles.summary: What a night. On Sunday, November 15, the winners of the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, celebrated together at Nine Orchard in NYC. More than 200 chefs, restaurateurs, bartenders, and friends of Eater — many of whom traveled across the country to be there — partook in live…

Now in its 17th year, the Eater Awards recognize the year’s best new restaurants, bakeries, bars, dishes, and chefs in markets across the U.S.. More than 30 Eater staffers and contributors spent months traveling to 44 cities to weigh contenders on food, service, atmosphere, and the stories behind them. The prize? A tomato can trophy. And yes, they’re real.

The night started off strong with photos at the tomato can-wrapped step-and-repeat and a welcome shot of Zbiotics, before guests headed up to the roof of Nine Orchard for panoramic views and more fun. The party was filled with unique moments, from custom lighter engraving presented by Toast to live water color portraits presented by Capital One. Rounds of dishes inspired by the winning restaurants were passed.

A champagne toast commemorated the resiliency of the hospitality industry. “Thank you for what you do, every single day, to bolster your team, your community, and the restaurant industry at large,” said Eater editor in chief Stephanie Wu.

articles.title: To Write ‘The Brightness,’ Chad Harbach Planned a Friends Trip to Block Island
articles.summary: While researching a pivotal, 150-page section of his new novel, the author returned to Block Island to reacquaint himself with its “rugged, natural beauty.”
body: This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books.

My then-partner and I organized a trip to Block Island with a large group of friends in the summer of 2016. We rented a big house and folks came from places like New York, Philadelphia, California, and Amsterdam. It felt like a wedding in that sense—everyone gathered for this joyous celebration in a beautiful place. We didn’t do all the terrible stuff to one another that’s maybe required for the juicy plot of a novel, but we did spend eight days cooking together, playing the piano, singing songs, drinking a lot, and staying up very late.

articles.title: 18 Family Resorts That Go Above and Beyond for Those With Babies and Toddlers
articles.summary: Whether you're dreaming of an African safari or a beachfront escape, these properties prove you don't have to put extraordinary travel on hold until your children are older.
body: I've traveled to some pretty far-flung places, but nothing could have prepared me for the logistical circus of vacationing with a baby. Four years and 30 countries later, my son Julian has taught me a thing or two about what makes a resort genuinely welcoming to its littlest guests. For starters, there’s a massive difference between a hotel that hands your kid a coloring book at check-in and one that has anticipated the thousands of little things that can make or break a family vacation.

The best resorts for infants and toddlers also understand that keeping littles happy isn’t a one-size-fits-all proposition. A baby might need a quiet nursery and a reliable nanny; a three-year-old might be thrilled to feed goats on an Austrian farm, explore a Japanese forest, or make plaster casts of lion tracks in the Kalahari. And parents? Sometimes we just want to eat dinner without having to negotiate with a tiny inquisitor.
points: Whether you're dreaming of an African safari or a beachfront escape, these properties prove you don't have to put extraordinary travel on hold until your children are older.

articles.title: How We Brought a Taste of Maine to Bon Appétit LIVE
articles.summary: From shucking oysters and making creamy lobster dip to baking wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, here’s how Visit Maine brought New England flavor to the event.
body: Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit Manager of Audience Strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed 2-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

Tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

The best shearling jackets and coats are the wardrobe solution to get through the snow storms, polar vortexes, and mind-numbingly cold temperatures we will certainly face. A puffer coat might seem like the most sensible choice in most of these scenarios, but shearling coats and jackets provide a little more polish to every look, while still offering the warmth necessary to tide us over until spring.

Shearling outerwear has long been a wardrobe essential. It’s sturdy, durable, and made to last forever in your coat closet. Their timeless reputation makes them the perfect investment piece, an important fact to consider when shopping for items that you can love and own for years, and perhaps pass down one day. You can find faux options, otherwise billed as fleece or teddy, that look and feel just as good as the real thing.
